source_text: Hoc enim dico, paenitentiam, quae per dei gratiam ostensa et indicta nobis in gratiam nos domino revocat, semel cognitam atque susceptam nunquam posthac iteratione delicti resignari oportere. Iam quidem nullum ignorantiae praetextum tibi patrocinatur, quod domino agnito praeceptisque eius admissis denique paenitentia delictorum functus rursus te in delicta restituis. Ita in quantum ignorantia segregaris, in tantum contumaciae adglutinaris. Nam si idcirco te deliquisse paenituerat, quia dominum coeperas timere, cur, quod metus gratia gessisti, rescindere maluisti, nisi quia metuere desisti? Neque enim timorem alia res quam contumacia subvertit. Cum etiam ignorantes dominum nulla exceptio tueatur ad poenam, quia deum in aperto constitutum et vel ex ipsis caelestibus bonis comprehensibilem ignorari non licet, quanto cognitum despici periculosum est? Despicit porro qui bonorum ac malorum intellectum ab illo consecutus quod intellegit fugiendum quodque iam fugit resumens intellectui suo, id est dei dono, contumeliam facit: respuit datorem, cum datum deserit, negat beneficum, cum beneficium non honorat. Quemadmodum ei potest placere cuius munus sibi displicet? Ita in dominum non modo contumax, sed etiam ingratus appare. Ceterum non leviter in dominum peccat qui, cum aemulo eius diabolo paenitentia renuntiasset et hoc nomine illum domino subiecisset rursus eundem regressu suo erigit et exultationem eius seipsum facit, ut denuo malus recuperata praeda sua adversus dominum gaudeat. Nonne, quod dicere quoque periculosum est, sed ad aedificationem proferendum est, diabolum domino praeponit? Comparationem enim videtur egisse qui utrumque cognoverit, et iudicato pronuntiasse eum meliorem cuius se rursus esse maluerit. Ita qui per delictorum paenitentiam instituerat domino satisfacere, diabolo per aliam paenitentiae paenitentiam satisfaciet, eritque tanto magis perosus deo, quanto aemulo eius acceptus. Sed aiunt quidam satis deum habere, si corde et animo suspiciatur, licet actu minus fiat; itaque se salvo metu et fide peccare, hoc est salva castitate matrimonia violare, salva pietate parenti venenum temperare. Sic ergo et ipsi salva venia in gehennam detrudentur, dum salvo metu peccant. Primum exemplum perversitatis: quia timent, delinquunt. Opinor, non delinquerent, si non timerent. Igitur qui deum nolit offensum, nec revereatur omnino, si timor offendendi patrocinium est. Sed ista ingenia de semine hypocritarum pullulare consuerunt, quorum individua cum diabolo amicitia est, quorum paenitentia nunquam fidelis.
thought_title: Repentance must not be undone by returning to sin
orientation: Tertullian is addressing Christians who have already come to know God and received repentance, warning them that returning to sin after repentance is defiance and ingratitude toward God.
pass_a_gloss: For this I say: repentance, which has been shown and commanded to us through God's grace and calls us back to the Lord into grace, once it has been known and taken up, ought never afterward to be undone by a repetition of sin. Now indeed no pretext of ignorance protects you, because, having known the Lord and having admitted his commands and finally having performed repentance of sins, you place yourself back into sins again. Thus, to the extent that you are separated from ignorance, to that extent you are glued to defiance. For if you had repented of having sinned for this reason, because you had begun to fear the Lord, why did you prefer to undo what you did for the sake of fear, unless because you stopped fearing? For no other thing than defiance overturns fear. Since even those who do not know the Lord are protected by no exception from punishment, because it is not permitted for God, who is set in the open and comprehensible even from the heavenly goods themselves, to be unknown, how much more dangerous is it for him to be despised once known? Moreover, he despises him who, having received from him the understanding of good and evil, by taking up again what he understands should be fled and what he has already fled, does insult to his own understanding, that is, to God's gift: he spurns the giver when he abandons the gift, he denies the benefactor when he does not honor the benefit. How can he please him whose gift displeases him? Thus you appear toward the Lord not only defiant, but also ungrateful. Moreover, he does not sin lightly against the Lord who, when he had renounced the devil, his rival, through repentance and by this name had subjected him to the Lord, again raises up the same one by his return and makes himself the devil's exultation, so that the evil one, having recovered his booty, rejoices against the Lord again. Does he not—which is also dangerous to say, but must be brought forward for edification—put the devil before the Lord? For he seems to have made a comparison who has known both, and by his judgment to have pronounced him better whose man he has preferred to be again. Thus he who had resolved through repentance of sins to make amends to the Lord will make amends to the devil through another repentance of repentance, and he will be that much more hated by God as he is accepted by his rival. But some say that God has enough if he is regarded with heart and soul, even if less is done in act; and so they say they sin with fear and faith intact, that is, with chastity intact to violate marriages, with piety intact to mix poison for a parent. Thus therefore they themselves will be thrust into hell with forgiveness intact, while they sin with fear intact. First example of perversity: because they fear, they sin. I think they would not sin if they did not fear. Therefore he who does not want God offended should not revere him at all, if fear of offending is a defense. But these dispositions have been accustomed to sprout from the seed of hypocrites, whose friendship with the devil is indivisible, whose repentance is never faithful.

choices.why: The verb means to unseal or cancel; 'undone' captures the reversal of a completed repentance without importing a technical term.
The verb is vivid and physical; 'glued' preserves the image of close attachment to defiance.
The glossary requires 'defiance' for contumacia, and it fits the argument that returning to sin is willful disobedience.
The glossary requires 'making amends' for satisfactio; the verb form is rendered consistently.
The ablative absolute 'salvo' means 'with X safe/intact'; the phrase is ironic, so 'intact' preserves the paradox.
The glossary requires 'hell' for gehenna; 'thrust' captures the force of detrudere.

pass_b_english: What I am saying is this: repentance, which God's grace has shown us and commanded us, and which calls us back into God's favor, must never be undone by repeating the sin once it has been recognized and accepted.

You no longer have any excuse of ignorance to defend you. After you have come to know the Lord, accepted his commands, and then carried out repentance for your sins, you have put yourself back into those sins again. To the degree that you are separated from ignorance, you are glued to defiance. For if you repented of your sin because you had begun to fear God, why did you choose to undo what you did out of fear, unless because you stopped fearing? Nothing but defiance overturns fear.

Even those who do not know the Lord have no exemption to protect them from punishment, because God stands in the open and can be understood from the very blessings of heaven, so it is not permitted to be ignorant of him. How much more dangerous is it to despise him once he is known? And the one who has received from him the understanding of good and evil despises him when he takes up again what he understands he should flee and what he has already fled. He insults his own understanding, which is God's gift. He rejects the giver when he abandons the gift; he denies the benefactor when he does not honor the benefit. How can he please the one whose gift displeases him? So you appear before the Lord not only defiant but also ungrateful.

Moreover, it is no light sin against the Lord when someone who had renounced the devil, God's rival, through repentance and in that name had subjected him to the Lord, raises that same devil up again by his return and makes himself the devil's exultation, so that the evil one rejoices against the Lord once more, having recovered his prey. Does he not put the devil before the Lord? It is dangerous even to say this, but it must be said for building up. The one who has known both seems to have made a comparison and, after judging, declared that the one he chose to belong to again is better. So the one who had begun to make amends to God through repentance for his sins will make amends to the devil through a repentance of repentance, and he will be that much more hated by God as he is accepted by God's rival.

But some people object: God is satisfied if he is honored in heart and soul, even if less is done in action. So they sin with fear and faith intact—that is, they violate marriages with chastity intact, they mix poison for a parent with piety intact. In the same way, they will be thrust into hell with forgiveness intact, while they sin with fear intact. This is the first example of their perversity: they sin because they fear. I think they would not sin if they did not fear. So the one who does not want God to be offended should not revere him at all, if fear of offending is a defense for sin. But these ideas usually sprout from the seed of hypocrites, whose friendship with the devil is inseparable, and whose repentance is never faithful.

last_rejected.quote: So the one who does not want God to be offended should not revere him at all, if fear of offending is a defense for sin.
last_rejected.source_quote: Igitur qui deum nolit offensum, nec revereatur omnino, si timor offendendi patrocinium est.
last_rejected.why: 'revereatur' here is negative: 'should not fear God at all.' English 'revere' inverts the sense.
last_rejected.fix: So the one who does not want God to be offended should not fear him at all, if fear of offending is a defense for sin.
last_rejected.ruling: Latin "nec revereatur omnino" = "and should not be reverenced/fear God at all"; English "should not revere him at all" matches.

polish.changed: Clarified the imagined objector's position in the final paragraph, kept the term 'defiance' consistent throughout, and smoothed sentence flow for reading aloud while preserving every claim and qualification.

notes.why: Three different English words for the related concept of willful contempt of God after knowing him; reader may miss the connection.
notes.fix: Distinguish 'defiance' (contempt after knowledge) from 'presumption' (taking forgiveness for granted) consistently.

notes.quote: But some people say that God is satisfied if he is honored in heart and soul, even if less is done in action.
notes.why: Reader cannot immediately tell this is an imagined objector's position being refuted, not Tertullian's own teaching.
notes.fix: Mark as an objection: 'But some people object, saying…'
